title: Wake-on-LAN magic packet
source: AMD, Magic Packet Technology (white paper 20213, 1995); SecureOn as implemented by network adapters since
about: Six octets of all ones, then the target adapter's hardware address sixteen times, and optionally a
SecureOn password of four or six octets. That is the whole format. A sleeping adapter looks for the
pattern anywhere in any frame it receives, so the packet has no header, no length and no type of its
own: it is carried as the payload of a UDP datagram to a broadcast address, by convention on port 9,
and none of that is the format's business.
What a description can refuse here is the pattern itself. A run of ones that is not all ones, or
sixteen copies that do not agree, is not a magic packet — no adapter would wake for it — so both are
checked on the way in rather than read as though they were right.

nodes.about: One format, sent and never answered. A machine that wakes says so by being there, not by replying.
Six octets of 0xFF. What an adapter scans for first; the address only counts after it.

nodes.because: The white paper fixes the synchronization stream at six octets of 0xFF.

about: The adapter's own hardware address, repeated sixteen times without a gap. One field rather than
sixteen: the copies are not separately meaningful, and an adapter matches the run as a whole.

nodes.purpose: The hardware address of the adapter to wake, as 'aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff'.

nodes.label: is the run one address said sixteen times?

about: An adapter configured for SecureOn will not wake without a password after the sixteenth copy, of
four octets or of six. Nothing in the packet says one is there and nothing measures it, so the
packet's own end is what says which: on the way in, the octets left over; on the way out, the
password the target was configured with. Those are three shapes, so three ways on — and no
fourth, which is how a packet with any other number of octets after the copies is refused.

nodes.about: The packet ends at the sixteenth copy. What an adapter without SecureOn is sent, and almost every magic packet.
A four-octet password, often written as an IPv4 address.
A six-octet password, often written as a hardware address.

nodes.purpose: The password the target adapter was configured with. A property of the adapter, kept between wakes — not something a caller restates per packet.

nodes.label: how long is the target's password?

edges.because: An adapter wakes for its own address said sixteen times. A run whose copies differ wakes nothing, so it is not read as though it would.
